abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Natural killer (NK) cells can protect from tumor‐transformed cells using a fine‐tuned machinery of activating and inhibiting receptors. An important activating receptor is Fc gamma receptor IIIa (FcγRIIIA or CD16A), which can trigger antibody‐dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) when recognizing antibody‐opsonized target cells. One strategy to boost ADCC responses may be achieved by inhibiting activation‐induced shedding of CD16A from the NK cell surface. However, previous preclinical studies have shown contrasting results regarding the effectiveness and limitations of this approach. Here, microchip‐based live cell‐imaging was used to assess the consequences of CD16A shedding inhibition on the dynamics of NK cell cytotoxicity. The bispecific innate cell engager acimtamig (AFM13) was superior to IgG1 monoclonal antibodies in ADCC and in increasing the fraction of cytotoxic NK cells and serial killers. Under conditions where CD16A shedding was inhibited, acimtamig still triggered ADCC; however, the ability to promote serial killing was reduced and associated with impaired NK cell detachment from target cells. These results demonstrate that CD16A shedding represents an intrinsic feature of NK cell biology that is critical to sustain the antitumoral cytotoxicity of NK cells. This has implications for CD16A engineering of NK cell products and their combination with CD16A‐directed NK cell engagers.

sec.p: Keywords: acimtamig, CD16 shedding, innate cell engager, microchip, NK cells, serial killing

abstract.p: NK cells kill tumor targets via antibody‐dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC), mediated by the receptor CD16A. We show that the bispecific innate cell engager acimtamig (AFM13) enhances ADCC and boosts NK cell serial killing. Live‐cell imaging revealed that CD16A shedding is essential for efficient NK cell detachment and sustained killing.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Natural killer (NK) cells respond to malignantly transformed and virus‐infected cells by direct cytotoxicity and release of pro‐inflammatory cytokines. NK cells can be divided into two main subsets based on their expression of CD56 and the IgG receptor FcγRIIIA (CD16A). CD56bright CD16A− NK cells show strong cytokine production, while CD56dim CD16A+ NK cells instead show strong cytotoxic activity and represent approximately 90% of circulating NK cells in blood and spleen [1, 2]. NK cells discriminate between healthy and diseased cells through a balance between inhibitory and activating signals, mediated by cell surface receptors. Important activating receptors include CD16A, NKG2D, DNAM‐1, and natural cytotoxicity receptors [3]. NK cell cytotoxicity is dependent on immune synapse formation—a tight intercellular junction between the NK cell and target cell—where the NK cell assembles its cytotoxic machinery, culminating in delivery of granules containing perforin and granzyme, or the presentation of death receptors [4, 5].

Upon cellular activation, the CD16A receptor can be cleaved from the cell surface of neutrophils and NK cells by the metalloprotease (MMP), a disintegrin and metalloprotease‐17 (ADAM‐17) or membrane type 6 matrix metalloproteinase [6, 7, 8]. CD16A shedding can also be induced by other stimuli, for example, NKG2D [9] or cytokines [10, 11, 12]. Therefore, a strategy to enhance antibody‐dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) by NK cells is to use molecular inhibitors or protein constructs that prevent shedding of CD16A [13, 14]. While this approach aims to maximize CD16A availability for ADCC [15, 16], and has shown increased cytokine production by NK cells [6, 17], studies have shown that inhibition of CD16A shedding can lead to impaired detachment from target cells, reducing the capacity for an individual NK cell to form serial contacts with target cells [17] and even induce NK cell death [9]. Altogether, the data have remained ambiguous regarding the overall consequences and dynamic changes associated with CD16A shedding inhibition.

Bispecific NK cell engagers have emerged as a successful strategy for increased immune cell activation and tumor cell killing [18, 19, 20, 21]. Engagers with specificity for the activating receptor CD16A can selectively trigger ADCC by NK cells or antibody‐dependent cellular phagocytosis (ADCP) by macrophages. The CD30/CD16A‐specific innate cell engager (ICE) acimtamig (AFM13) has shown efficacy in patients with CD30+ lymphomas as a monotherapy [22], in combination with the checkpoint inhibitor, pembrolizumab [23], and in combination with adoptive NK cell therapy [24].

Here, live cell imaging with single‐cell resolution was used to assess how stimulation with ICE molecules affects the dynamics of NK cell cytotoxicity and the impact of CD16A shedding in these processes. We show that high‐affinity CD16A engagement by acimtamig can increase both the fraction of cytotoxic NK cells and the number of target cells killed by individual NK cells (serial killing). The elevated fraction of cytotoxic NK cells induced by ICE molecules is largely conserved under conditions when CD16A shedding is inhibited. However, analysis of the functional dynamics of NK cells in combination with acimtamig reveals that inhibition of CD16A shedding impairs NK cell detachment from target cells, resulting in cell cluster formation, reduced NK cell motility, and decreased NK cell viability. Together, these factors lead to reduced NK cell serial killing. Although shedding inhibition might be effective in the short term, it can impact sequential targeting of tumor cells and decrease the viability of individual NK cells and, therefore, limit the overall antitumoral activity.

sec.title: Acimtamig Induces Potent NK Cell Responses Against CD30‐Expressing Target Cells
sec.p: The CD30‐targeting ICE acimtamig has previously been shown to efficiently induce cytotoxic activity of NK cells toward CD30‐expressing target cells via ADCC [24, 25, 26]. Here, those results are corroborated and show that, compared with CD30 mAb or an antibody containing S239D and I332E modifications to increase CD16 binding (here called CD30 Enh‐mAb) [26, 27, 28], acimtamig induced significantly greater NK cell degranulation and IFNγ productionagainst the CD30high and CD30low expressing cell lines Karpas‐299 and Nalm‐6, respectively (Figure 1A,B; Figure S1A–C).

SD, standard deviation; w/o, without.

sec.p: To investigate the concentration dependence and kinetics of bulk NK cell‐induced ADCC, the Incucyte live‐cell analysis system was used (Figure 1C–G). NK cell cytotoxicity against Karpas‐299 and Nalm‐6 in the presence of acimtamig, CD30 mAb, or CD30 Enh‐mAb was induced in a dose‐dependent manner (Figure 1D,E; Figure S1D–E), where acimtamig induced a cytotoxic response at significantly lower concentrations compared with IgG antibodies for both target cells (Figure S1F,G). Stimulation with an anti‐CD16 mAb targeting the same anti‐CD16A domain as acimtamig and with a silenced Fc part, making it unable to induce ADCC, showed no NK cell activation. Kinetics analyses showed that a significant part of the acimtamig‐induced killing was happening within the first hour for Karpas‐299, while the kinetics of Nalm‐6 killing were slower (Figure 1F,G; Figure S1H,I).

In summary, in the presence of acimtamig, NK cell cytotoxicity against CD30high‐ and CD30low‐expressing tumor cells was induced in a dose‐ and time‐dependent manner, with superior potency when compared with wild‐type and Fc‐enhanced IgG molecules.

sec.title: Acimtamig Increases the Fraction of Cytotoxic NK Cells and Boosts Serial Killing
sec.p: To assess the cytotoxic potential of individual NK cells, microchip‐based live cell screening was performed (Figure 2A) [29]. Fluorescently labelled primary human NK cells and target cells were seeded into microwells of the chip, aiming for on average one NK cell and four target cells in each well. Once settled, the number of cells and their viability status in each well was assessed every hour by microscopy. Acimtamig stimulation triggered a significantly higher fraction of cytotoxic NK cells both toward Karpas‐299 and Nalm‐6 target cells compared with untreated controls (Figure 2B; Figure S2). Next, acimtamig was compared with CD30 mAb and CD30 Enh‐mAb. Against CD30high Karpas‐299 target cells, both acimtamig and CD30 Enh‐mAb induced a significantly higher fraction of cytotoxic NK cells compared with CD30 mAb and control (Figure 2C). However, against CD30low Nalm‐6 target cells, acimtamig triggered NK cell cytotoxicity significantly above CD30 Enh‐mAb (Figure 2D).

In (B) bars indicate the mean value and SD from n = 3 (Karpas‐299) and n = 5 (Nalm‐6) independent experiments, statistics performed with paired t‐test. Ab, antibody; NK, natural killer; PDMS, polydimethylsiloxane; SD, standard deviation.

sec.p: Our microchip‐based live cell imaging system is particularly suitable to assess the NK cell serial killing capacity, by selectively analyzing microwells containing a single NK cell with multiple (here set to ≥3) target cells (Figure 2E). Against Karpas‐299, both acimtamig and CD30 Enh‐mAb showed elevated fractions of NK cells performing multiple kills, while only acimtamig had that effect in Nalm‐6 cells (Figure 2F–H). When depicting the fraction of cytotoxic NK cells that killed at least three target cells (serial killers), this became even more evident (Figure 2G–I).
These data demonstrate that high‐affinity engagement of CD16A by acimtamig increases the fraction of cytotoxic NK cells and boosts the fraction of serial killers against CD30‐expressing target cells.

sec.title: Acimtamig‐Induced Serial Killing Is Decreased by Inhibition of CD16A Shedding
sec.p: The effect of CD16A shedding on serial engagement of target cells by NK cells was investigated using our microchip technology (Figure 3). CD16A shedding was inhibited by exposing human primary NK cells to Batimastat, a broad‐spectrum MMP inhibitor, while interacting with CD30intermediate target cells (Figure S1A), HL‐60, or CD30low target cells Nalm‐6 (Figure 3A–F,G–K, respectively). In agreement with previous studies [25, 30], the flow cytometry experiment confirmed that Batimastat inhibited CD16 shedding on NK cells cocultured with Nalm‐6 target cells in the presence of acimtamig (Figure S3A). HL‐60 target cells were introduced since Batimastat treatment was toxic to Karpas‐299 target cells. Similar toxicity was not observed in the other two target cell lines or in the NK cells (Figure S3B,C). With HL‐60 target cells, acimtamig treatment increased the fraction of time spent in conjugates, and inhibition of CD16A shedding increased that fraction further (Figure 3B). This appeared to be due to impaired detachment between NK and target cells since NK cells commonly remained in conjugation with killed target cells, resulting in the formation of large clusters of cells (Figure 3A). Similarly, when NK cells were incubated with the adherent epidermal growth factor (EGFR)‐expressing cell line DK‐MG together with the EGFR/CD16 bispecific ICE AFM24 and Batimastat, large clusters of target cells were formed around the NK cells (Figure S3D), and a significant increase in the fraction of NK cells involved in long‐lasting contacts was observed (Figure S3E). For the CD30low target Nalm‐6, the fraction of time in conjugation was not significantly elevated (Figure 3G).

Blue arrows indicate the position of the NK cells, while white arrows mark dying target cells. Time is shown as hour:minutes, and the scale bar represents 50 µm. (B) Fraction of time NK cells spent in conjugates with HL‐60 target cells. (C) Percentage of cytotoxic NK cells against HL‐60. (D) Distribution of the number of kills performed by individual NK cells against HL‐60. (E) Fraction of serial killers against HL‐60. (F) Percentage of NK cells that died after killing HL‐60 target cells. (G) Fraction of time NK cells spent in conjugates with Nalm‐6 target cells. (H) Percentage of cytotoxic NK cells against Nalm‐6. (I) Distribution of the number of kills performed by individual NK cells against Nalm‐6. (J) Fraction of serial killers against Nalm‐6. (K) Percentage of NK cells that died after killing Nalm‐6 target cells. Graphs show mean values with SD from n = 5 or n = 4 independent donors for HL‐60 and NALM‐6, respectively. Concentration of acimtamig used was 9.4 nM. Data in (E) and (J) are presented as super plots, color‐coded according to donor, where data from individual NK cells are shown in the background with median presented as colored dots, a middle black bar representing the mean of medians, and error bars representing the SD. Statistical tests used were multiple comparison one‐way ANOVA, where sphericity was assumed in (B, C, E, F, H, and J), while a Geisser–Greenhouse correction was used in (G) and (K). *p ≤ 0.05, **p ≤ 0.01, ***p ≤ 0.001, ****p ≤ 0.0001. BAT, Batimastat; SD, standard deviation.

sec.p: NK cells efficiently killed HL‐60 target cells, and the number of cytotoxic cells increased with acimtamig irrespective of Batimastat co‐treatment (Figure 3C). Conversely, the fraction of cytotoxic NK cells responding to Nalm‐6 target cells upon co‐treatment of acimtamig and Batimastat showed a decreasing trend (Figure 3H). As suggested in previous reports [9, 17], we here show that inhibition of CD16A shedding affected the cytotoxic potential of individual NK cells (Figure 3D,I). Acimtamig‐induced NK cell serial killing was reduced in the presence of Batimastat (Figure 3D,E,I,J). Furthermore, in line with previous reports [9], it was observed that the fraction of NK cells that died after performing killing was elevated when treated with Batimastat (Figure 3F,K).

These results show that inhibition of CD16A shedding does not reduce the fraction of acimtamig‐triggered cytotoxic NK cells but leads to impaired NK cell detachment, which impedes serial killing and possibly lowers NK cell viability.

sec.title: Expression of a Noncleavable CD16A Reduces Acimtamig‐Induced NK Serial Killing
sec.p: Next, a Batimastat‐independent system using variants of the NK92 NK cell line overexpressing either noncleavable high‐affinity CD16A (NK92 HA‐NC) or cleavable high‐affinity CD16A (NK92 HA) [31, 32] was used. Consistent with these CD16A variants, NK92 HA showed CD16A downregulation in response to susceptible HL‐60 target cells, both in the absence and presence of acimtamig, suggesting that cleavable CD16A is effectively downregulated also by the ADCC‐independent activation of the NK cells. In contrast, little downregulation was observed for noncleavable NK92 HA‐NC (Figure 4A,B). The residual decrease of CD16A in the presence of acimtamig in noncleavable NK92 HA‐NC may be suggestive of an alternative mechanism for downregulation, for example, internalization [33].

Data in (D) are presented as a super plot, color‐coded according to experiment, where data from individual NK cells are shown in the background with median presented as colored dots, a middle black bar representing the mean of medians, and error bars representing the SD. The statistical tests used were multiple comparison two‐way ANOVA with assumed sphericity (B), one‐way ANOVA where sphericity was assumed (D), one‐way ANOVA with Geisser–Greenhouse correction was used in (E), and a nonparametric test (Friedman test) was used in (G) and (H). *p ≤ 0.05, **p ≤ 0.01, ***p ≤ 0.001, ****p ≤ 0.0001. sec.p: A similar analysis of CD16A expression after interaction with Karpas‐299 and Nalm‐6 target cells was also performed (Figure S4A). For NK92 HA, CD16A was downregulated in an acimtamig‐dependent fashion for Karpas‐299, but only to a small extent for Nalm‐6, both with and without acimtamig. CD16A downregulation in NK92 HA‐NC did occur for Karpas‐299 treated with acimtamig, supporting the presence of an additional mechanism for downregulation besides shedding.

All three NK92 cell lines were also evaluated in a standard 4 h degranulation (CD107a) assay (Figure S4B). NK92 HA and HA‐NC showed similar degranulation trends for Karpas‐299, HL‐60, and Nalm‐6, with increased degranulation in the presence of acimtamig to varying extent. Due to the possible internalization process in Karpas‐299, we chose Nalm‐6 and HL‐60 for microchip‐based live cell imaging.

The dynamics and cytotoxicity of NK92 HA and NK92 HA‐NC cells were assessed in microwell chip experiments using NK92 cells co‐incubated with HL‐60 (Figure 4C–H) or Nalm‐6 cells (Figure S5) with or without acimtamig. Both NK92 cell line variants spent a large fraction (>80%) of time in conjugation with HL‐60 target cells (Figure 4D) and showed high (>90%) cytotoxicity (Figure 4E). For Nalm‐6, the fractions of times in conjugates were lower (<50%) in all conditions (Figure S5A), while the fraction of cytotoxic cells varied between 45%–80%, with a significant increase when introducing acimtamig to NK92 HA (Figure S5B). A majority of NK92 cells killed multiple HL‐60 targets independent of condition, with a shift in distribution between cleavable and noncleavable CD16A in the presence of acimtamig (Figure 4F). Consistently, serial killing was reduced for NK92 HA‐NC cells in combination with acimtamig (Figure 4G). For Nalm‐6, serial killing increased moderately with the addition of acimtamig (Figure S5C,D). NK viability showed minor differences between conditions for HL‐60 (Figure 4H) but decreased for Nalm‐6 when acimtamig was introduced (Figure S5E), in particular, for NK92 NC‐HA. Thus, in our system expression of cleavable CD16A can increase the effector's ability to perform serial killing.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Serial killing is an important characteristic of NK cell cytotoxicity, and in vitro experiments have shown that a low fraction of effective NK cells can be responsible for a majority of the target cell killing [34, 35]. Serial killing requires an NK cell to repeatedly locate, recognize, and kill new target cells. The factors that are essential for serial killing have not been completely elucidated, but limiting factors could be NK cell motility, maintenance of activating signaling, repeated mobilization of the cytotoxic machinery, and effective detachment from previous target cells. Often, the majority of the NK cells in a population will not perform multiple kills and may not become activated by a certain tumor target cell [34, 35]. Antibody‐based NK cell engagers have proven an effective approach to increase the fraction of NK cells capable of launching a response against otherwise “invisible” tumor target cells [18, 19, 20, 21]. While the recognition and cytotoxic phases of killing have been described [4], the disassembly of the immune synapse and disengagement are less well understood, although some studies have been published in recent years [36, 37]. Further understanding of NK cell viability and function is of particular importance for the development of approaches to increase NK cell responses in the clinic.

In this study, we used a microwell chip assay to show that the bispecific acimtamig potently increases NK‐cell activation compared with two monoclonal antibodies targeting the same CD30 epitope. These results indicate that the high‐affinity engagement of CD16A by acimtamig is superior to CD30 Enh‐mAb, leading to increased fractions of cytotoxic cells and serial killing against CD30‐expressing target cells. The strong killing response at low concentrations of acimtamig could represent a clinical advantage, providing the opportunity for quantitative clearance of malignantly transformed cells, which might otherwise give rise to residual disease and relapse.

It is well established that NK cell activation leads to MMP‐induced shedding of CD16A [6, 13], thus potentially leading to a decreased ability for NK cells to maintain activating signaling through this receptor in sequential encounters with target cells. However, when using the broad MMP inhibitor, Batimastat, serial killing was decreased, both for HL‐60 and Nalm‐6, with no or small differences observed in the fraction of cytotoxic NK cells. For HL‐60, this was accompanied by an increased fraction of time NK cells spent in conjugation with target cells and the formation of large cell clusters around the effectors. Long‐lasting conjugation and cluster formation were even more pronounced when using the adherent target cell line DK‐MG in combination with the CD16/EGFR bispecific ICE, AFM24. NK92 cells killed HL‐60 target cells very effectively, with high frequencies of cytotoxic cells and serial killers, also without the addition of acimtamig. Despite this background killing, it was observed that serial killing was reduced for the NK92 cell line expressing the noncleavable version of CD16A in combination with acimtamig. This difference was, however, not observed for the target cell line Nalm‐6. Together, these results show that the strong affinity induced by the ICE molecules in combination with inhibition of CD16 shedding can lead to impaired NK cell detachment and decreased serial killing. Thus, these data corroborate that some level of shedding of CD16A is an integral part of the disassembly of the immune synapse that is important for repeated killing by individual NK cells [9, 17].

Overall, our results are in line with previous findings, mainly based on flow cytometry or bulk cytotoxicity data, that have shown that CD16A shedding inhibition boosts cytokine production by NK cells but generally show small differences in the fraction of degranulating NK cells [6, 17, 38]. Hyperproduction of cytokines has been observed in situations where NK cell detachment is impaired, leading to abnormally long contacts with target cells [36, 37] and even connected to severe pathological effects. In this study, increased NK cell death was observed as another consequence of shedding inhibition with Batimastat. Batimastat‐induced NK cell death was also observed in cocultures with HL‐60 in the absence of acimtamig. This indicates that, in addition to CD16A, other surface proteins involved in the immune synapse are clipped off by the metalloprotease during detachment, giving further support that receptor shedding is an integral process during termination of cell–cell contacts. Thus, although inhibition of shedding might be effective in the short term, its complete abolishment can impact sustained targeting of distant tumor cells and, by this, limit the overall antitumoral activity.

Patients with functional ADAM17 deficiency have suffered from recurrent bacterial infections and hyperinflammation, which have been associated with premature death [39, 40]. Thus, it is unclear if ADAM17 inhibition may have any clinical benefits. To our knowledge, clinical translation of ADAM17 inhibitors in the context of engaging CD16A has not yet shown a pronounced clinical benefit. Bachanova et al. [41] reported a clinical study where the ADAM17 inhibitor INCB7839 was utilized in combination with Rituximab as a posttransplant consolidation strategy in patients with diffuse large B‐cell lymphoma. This study showed a difference in soluble CD16, a potential impact measurement of the ADAM17 inhibitor, and demonstrated a 97% overall survival in the test group, compared with 95% with Rituximab treatment alone in a similar cohort, over 1 year. Furthermore, the introduction of cleavage‐resistant CD16A through genetic modification of iPSC‐derived NK cells is currently being pursued by various investigators with no evaluable and comparative clinical data reported yet. Since systemic administration of ADAM17 inhibitors requires management of side effects [42], which may also be true for iPSC‐derived NK cells expressing cleavage‐resistant CD16A, risk‐benefit analyses in further prospective clinical trials are warranted.

In summary, our data show that ADCC induced by acimtamig leads to efficient NK‐cell‐mediated killing of CD30‐expressing tumor target cells with an important contribution of serial killing. This serial killing and overall NK‐cell survival are facilitated by maintaining the ability of NK cells to efficiently detach from target cells. Thus, despite a potential decrease in the recognition of target cells after sequential killing, overall and long‐term responses by NK cells may be augmented by naturally occurring shedding of CD16A.

sec.title: Cell Culture
sec.p: Human NK cells were isolated from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from anonymous healthy donors provided by the Karolinska University Hospital, Sweden, or the DRK‐Blutspendedienst Baden‐Württemberg‐Hessen, Mannheim, Germany. PBMCs were isolated using Ficoll gradient, and aliquots were frozen at −80°C containing 100 million PBMCs or incubated overnight. NK cells were enriched from frozen or fresh PBMC preparations using negative selection kits (Cat. No. 130‐092‐657, Miltenyi Biotec or Cat. No. 19055, STEMCELL Technologies) according to the manufacturer's instructions. NK cells were maintained in DMEM cell culture media (Sigma‐Aldrich) supplemented with 30% Ham's F12, 10% human serum (Sigma‐Aldrich), 50 U/mL penicillin–streptomycin, 2 mM L‐glutamine, 1× nonessential amino acids, 1 mM sodium pyruvate (all from Sigma‐Aldrich), and 100 U/mL IL‐2 (Peprotech) stimulation for 2 days. Based on analysis from three independent donors, 93.4 ± 4.6% of the NK cells expressed CD16. The leukemia cell lines Karpas‐299 (Cat. No. 06072604‐1VL, Sigma‐Aldrich), Nalm‐6 cells (Cat. No ACC128, DSMZ), leukemia cell line HL‐60 (Cat. No ACC3, DSMZ), and human glioblastoma DK‐MG cells (Cat. No ACC277, DSMZ) were cultured in RPMI 1640 media supplemented with 10% FBS, and 50 U/mL penicillin–streptomycin (all from Sigma‐Aldrich). NK92 cell lines were generated from NK92 WT (Cat. No. CRL‐2407, ATCC) as described in the supporting information and cultured in stem cell growth medium (SCGM, Cat. No. 20802‐0500, CellGenix) supplemented with 20% FBS, which was enriched with 300 U/mL IL‐2 every second day.

sec.title: Generation of NK92 Cell Lines
sec.p: To generate NK92 cells with high‐affinity (HA) or high‐affinity noncleavable (HA NC) CD16, the LeGO‐G2 plasmid (Cat.No.25917 Addgene) was modified by adding a multiple cloning site (MCS) from pcDNA3 (Cat. No.13032 Addgene), a T2A sequence, and a linker (amino acids GSGSGSG) in frame with downstream eGFP. The CD16A sequence was retrieved from Uniprot (P08637), and Phenylalanine 158 was replaced with Valine (HA) and Serine 197 with Phenylalanine (NC) [43]. These sequences were codon‐optimized using GenSmart (Genscript), and the synthesized sequences were cloned into the MCS of the LeGO‐G2 plasmid using BamHI and XbaI restriction sites. NK92 Mock contained the empty vector. All plasmids were verified by sequencing (Eurofins). Lentivirus was produced as previously described [44]. Briefly, 1 × 106 HEK293FT cells (Cat. No. CRL‐3216, ATCC) were plated into a poly‐D‐lysine‐coated 150 mm dish (Corning). On the following day, the cells were transfected with 30 µg of the cloned transfer plasmids encoding CD16‐HA/NC, 15 µg of pMDLg/pRRE (Cat. No.12251, Addgene), 10 µg of pRSV‐REV (Cat. No.12553, Addgene), and 5 µg of phCMV‐VSV‐G (Cat. No. 8454, Addgene) using a calcium phosphate transfection kit (Sigma‐Aldrich) in the presence of 25 µM chloroquine (Sigma‐Aldrich). The medium was changed 16 h posttransfection, and the virus particles were collected after an additional 28 h, by filtering the supernatant through a 0.45 µm filter and then stored at −80°C. Thirty thousand NK92 cells were suspended in 150 µL SCGM medium supplemented with 20% FBS in flat‐bottom 96‐well plates. Cells were transduced at a multiplicity of infection of 8, for 6 h in 8 µg/mL protamine sulphate (Sigma Aldrich) and 7 µM 5Z‐7‐Oxozeaenol (Bio‐Techne Tocris). After transduction, cells were cultured for 4 days and then stained using BV421‐conjugated anti‐human CD16A antibody (BioLegend) to confirm the expression level.

sec.title: Antibodies and Inhibitors
sec.p: The bispecific cell engagers and antibodies tested in this work were produced in‐house by Affimed. CD30/CD16A bispecific engager acimtamig [26], anti‐CD30 wildtype monoclonal IgG antibody (CD30 mAb), double mutant S239D/I332E anti‐CD30 Fc‐enhanced monoclonal IgG antibody (CD30 Enh‐mAb) [26, 27, 28], anti‐CD16A monoclonal antibody, and the EGFR/CD16A bispecific engager AFM24 [45] were used at the concentrations indicated in the respective figures. Batimastat (Cat. No. SML0041, Sigma‐Aldrich) was used at a final concentration of 10 µM.

sec.title: Incucyte Assay
sec.p: Target cells were labeled with 2 µM Cytolight Red Dye (Cat. No. 4706, Sartorius) or Cytolight Orange Dye (Cat. No. 4839, Sartorius) in PBS (Cat. No. 14190‐094, Gibco) for 20 min at a cell density of 4 × 105/mL. NK cells were seeded into a flat‐bottom 96‐well plate (5 × 104 in 50 µL per well) and co‐cultured with labelled target cells (1 × 104 in 50 µL per well). Antibody constructs were added at the indicated concentrations. Incucyte Annexin V green Dye (Cat.No. 4642, Sartorius) was added at a final volume dilution of 1:800. All cells and reagents were prepared in MEM alpha (Cat. No. 22571‐020, Gibco) assay medium at 200 µL/well final volume, followed by incubation in the Incucyte instrument at 37°C, 5% CO2. Image acquisition was performed every hour for up to 8 h using the “non‐adherent cell‐by‐cell” module with the following parameters: 20× objective, 4 images/well, channels: phase contrast, red/orange, and green channel, acquisition time: green channel 300 ms; red/orange channel 400 ms. The nonadherent cell‐by‐cell analysis tool was used to quantify tumor cell killing of target cells based on the number of objects double‐positive for Cytolight red/orange and Annexin V green. Results were normalized to the total number of Cytolight red/orange single‐positive object counts in the corresponding well. Tumor cell killing in the absence of antibodies was used as controls.

sec.title: Flow Cytometry
sec.p: To assess NK cell activity, primary NK cells and target cells were co‐cultured at a 1:1 cell ratio (each 1 × 105/well) in the presence of anti‐human CD107a‐FITC (final dilution 1:100, clone H4A3, Cat. No. 328606, Biolegend) in round‐bottom 96‐well plates. Co‐cultures were supplemented with 10‐fold serial dilutions of indicated antibody constructs at final concentrations of 3, 0.3, 0.03, or 0.003 µg/mL. Cells were centrifuged at 300 rcf for 2 min and incubated for 30 min. After addition of GolgiPlug/Brefeldin A (final dilution 1:1000, Cat. No. 555029, BD Biosciences), cells were incubated for 3.5 h at 37°C and 5% CO2 before CD107a and IFNγ expression was assessed by flow cytometry.

Extracellular staining was performed in FACS buffer (PBS with 2% FCS and 0.05% sodium azide, Sigma‐Aldrich), including fixable Viability Dye‐eFluor 780 (1:2000; Cat. No. 65‐0865‐14, Thermo Fisher Scientific) on ice for 30 min in the dark, followed by washing in FACS buffer. Afterwards, intracellular staining was performed using the Cyto‐Fast Perm/Wash‐Buffer kit (Cat. No. 426803, Biolegend) for 30 min in the dark at room temperature. Cells were washed in FACS buffer and analyzed on a CytoFlexS flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter). The following fluorescent monoclonal antibodies were used: CD16A BV421 (1:100; clone 3G8, Cat. No. 302038, Biolegend); CD56 PE‐Cy7 (1:50; clone 5.1H11, Cat. No. 362510, Biolegend); CD45 BV785 (1:100; clone HI30, Cat. No. 304048, Biolegend), CD3 BV510 (1:100; clone UCHT‐1 Cat. No. 300448, Biolegend) anti‐human IFNγ PE (1:100; clone B27, Cat. No. 506507, Biolegend). The gating strategy for NK cells is shown in Figure S6.

To assess CD16A expression and degranulation of NK92 NK cells, CD107a assays followed by CD16A immunostaining were performed using NK92 Mock, NK92 HA, and NK92 HA‐NC cells as effectors. Assays were conducted as previously described, but in the absence of GolgiPlug/Brefeldin A. The following antibodies were used for CD107a assays and immunostainings: mouse anti‐human CD107a Brilliant Violet 421 (final dilution: 1:100, clone: H4A3, Biolegend), mouse anti‐human CD16A APC (final dilution: 1:100, clone 3G8, BD Bioscience). Cell viability was assessed by staining the cell suspension in Fixable Viability Stain 510 (BD Bioscience) diluted in PBS (1:1000) for 15 min at room temperature, followed by two washing steps.

sec.title: Design and Fabrication of Microwell Chip and Holder
sec.p: Three different types of microwell chips that had different microwell dimensions were used. Two of the chip types had 300 µm deep, hexagonally shaped microwells that were either 60 or 80 µm in width [46]. The microwells were distributed in four separate honeycomb arrays, each made of 36 subarrays. The footprint of such a subarray matched the imaging field‐of‐view when using a 10× magnification lens on a 13 × 13 mm2 sensor in the microscope. The chip with 60 µm wells included 224 wells in each subarray and 32,256 wells in total on the chip, and the chip with 80 µm wells included 143 wells in each subarray and 20,592 wells in total on the chip. These two types of chips were assembled in a chip holder that had the shape and dimensions of a standard culture dish to fit in a conventional microscope stage insert. The holder included a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) gasket and a top part that included four open liquid media chambers. When the holder and the chip were assembled, the media chambers aligned with the four main well arrays on the chip. The third type of chip had 300 µm deep and 350 µm wide microwells distributed in a layout with 16 arrays, a design and fabrication that is described in earlier work [47]. All three types of microwell chips were fabricated using similar processes. In short, lithography and deep reactive ion etching were applied to form micro‐holes in Si that were closed by anodic bonding to a bottom glass substrate to form glass‐Si microwells. The glass bottom in the microwells had a thickness of 170 µm, corresponding to a #1.5H coverslip glass, for high optical quality and microscopy. The chip with 60 µm wells was used for assays with suspension cells, and the chips with the larger 80 and 350 µm wells were used with adherent cells.

sec.title: Microscopy Imaging Assays
sec.p: For fluorescent staining, cells were washed, incubated with 2.5 µM for CellTrace Yellow (Cat. No. C34567, Thermo Fisher Scientific; NK cells), 0.25 µM CellTrace Far Red (Cat. No. C34564, Thermo Fisher Scientific; Target cells) dissolved in PBS for 20 min at 37°C, washed, and used for experiments. SYTOX Green Nucleic Acid Stain (50 nM, Cat. No. S7020, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was present in the medium during the assay as a death indicator for both target and effector cells.

For cytotoxic assays, microwell chips with either 60, 80, or 350 µm wells were used as previously described [46, 47]. Briefly, target cells were seeded and a first set of images was acquired to record dead cells before starting the cytotoxic assay. Next, effector cells were seeded, and after a washing step, cell medium containing the compound(s) of interest was added and time‐lapse imaging was started (1, 10, or 20 frames/h for 12 h). For 60 and 80 µm seeding was optimized to have as many wells as possible containing a single NK and an effector:target ratio of 1:4. For 350 µm wells, DK‐MG targets cells were seeded and left for 48 h, before NK cells were added to achieve an E:T of 1:5–1:10.

All images were acquired on a Zeiss Colibri 7 wide‐field inverted microscope (Carl Zeiss, Germany) equipped with Plan‐Apochromat objectives (10× or 20×) and an incubation chamber kept at 37°C and 5% CO2.

sec.title: Image Analysis
sec.p: Microwell cytotoxicity screening data was analyzed automatically to enumerate the number of live/dead cells in each well at all time points. Image processing and cell quantifications were performed by a custom‐built MATLAB script previously described [29], now updated with adaptions to allow for identification of noncircular cells and effector cell death, as well as strategies to compensate for fluorescence bleed‐over and processes to compensate for fluorescence intensity variations over time. Briefly, images were first processed to identify the microwells using the transilluminated channel. Background subtraction was applied to the fluorescent channels by thresholding and remaining objects were smoothed and filtered to remove small objects. A watershed‐based algorithm (part of the MATLAB Imaging Toolbox) was then applied for segmentation of connected components to allow identification of individual cells. Cell identification was based on cell permanent (live) stain and the subsequent classification of live/dead was performed by manual gating on the live and dead fluorescence intensities measured within objects. All identified cells were mapped within their corresponding well together with temporal information about status.

For some experiments extensive clustering made it difficult to enumerate cells, and for some target cell lines, the SYTOX green dye was not reliably detecting dead cells, therefore, data from those experiments were analyzed manually with aid of ImageJ. Manual analysis was also used for experiments involving dynamics readouts, for example, contact times.

In general, wells with one live NK cell at the beginning of the assay were selected for analysis. Wells were excluded if a second live NK cell appeared in the well within the first 2 h of the assay and/or the NK cell died before interacting with target cells. For calculating the fraction of cytotoxic NK cells, wells with one or more live target cells at the beginning of the assay were selected for analysis, and the number of wells containing dead target cells was divided by the total number of selected cells. For serial killing analysis, wells with four or more live target cells at the beginning of the assay were selected for analysis. The fraction of serial killers was calculated by dividing the number of NK cells killing at least three (for primary NK cells) or four (for NK92 cells) target cells by the total number of cytotoxic cells (NK cells killing one or more target cells) from the selected wells. NK cell cytotoxicity was compensated for background death obtained from wells without effectors. The contacts between the effector and each target cell were scored, and the fraction of time in conjugation was calculated as the total time an NK cell spent in conjugation with one or multiple target cells, divided by the total time of observation. In cases when the NK cell died during the assay, the total observation time was up until that point. For the contact analysis, 40 primary NK cells per condition per experiment were analyzed, while for the NK92 experiments the corresponding number was 30 cells.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Data and statistical analysis were performed using Prism (GraphPad, La Jolla). To compare two groups with matching donors, a paired t‐test was conducted. To compare four groups and multiple matching donors, one‐way ANOVA was performed using the “Repeated Measures ANOVA Calculator” to validate the method's parameters [48]. If residuals followed a normal distribution and sphericity was not violated, sphericity was assumed and the Geisser–Greenhouse correction applied. In both cases, the Tukey test was used for multiple comparisons. When residuals did not follow a normal distribution, a nonparametric test (Friedman test) with Dunn's test for multiple comparisons was used instead. Only significant values were shown, and they were indicated with *p ≤ 0.05, **p ≤ 0.01, ***p ≤ 0.001, and ****p ≤ 0.0001.
